sources.claim: A 200MP Galaxy S23 Ultra shot is binned to a 12MP final image by default; binning combines up to 16 pixels; megapixels tell 'how much', not 'how good'; Galaxy S22 Ultra and OnePlus Nord N30 both have 108MP sensors but photos are 'not even close', the S22 Ultra having a larger sensor and larger pixels

A larger pixel can capture more light than a smaller pixel; binned night photos are brighter with reduced noise; Samsung 200MP HP2 sixteen-in-one is comparable to a 12.5MP camera with 2.56-micron pixels
Two sensors with the same megapixel count can have very different quality; sensor and photosite size matter more; in low light pixels are binned together to combine their light-gathering abilities

post.instagram_caption:
A 200 megapixel phone camera usually saves a 12 megapixel photo.

By default, Samsung's Galaxy S23 Ultra merges up to 16 tiny pixels into one bigger one, a trick called pixel binning, and saves a 12MP image (TechRadar). Bigger pixels catch more light, so night shots come out brighter and less grainy (Android Authority).

TechRadar also compared two phones with the same 108MP count and found the photos were not even close: the one with the larger sensor won.

The lesson: megapixels tell you how much, not how good. Look at sensor size first.

Source: TechRadar, Android Authority, How-To Geek.

post.youtube_description:
A 200 megapixel phone camera like the Galaxy S23 Ultra saves a 12 megapixel photo by default. It merges up to 16 tiny pixels into one bigger one, called pixel binning, because bigger pixels catch more light. Two phones with the same 108MP count can take very different photos, because sensor size matters more.
